blocks.text: Conclusion. In the Talmud passage cited in the preceding article, mention is made of the maggot that arises from mixed bran. Since express reference is made here to the kneading or mixing (גביל) of the bran, what is meant here is not the well-known mealworms or flour mites that arise in old flour; rather, here too it is a kind of maggot that develops from the spoiled bran.
The Dung Maggot.

Since the black raven is unloving toward its young (on this erroneous belief see §. 205), Providence cares for the latter by letting maggots arise from their own dung (B. batra 8a). Raschi on Erubin 22a explains it more simply, according to which Providence brings gnats to the young ravens, which is already logically more correct, since the ravens cannot excrete dung without having previously taken food, and where would this food come from, which was only supposed to arise from the dung? That worms arise from animal excrement is, moreover, common knowledge.
Helminths.

Whereas the Talmud mentions only a few species from the realm of parasites, such as the lice on the human body and the whale louse, from the realm of the helminths, i.e. those worms that live in other animal organisms, it mentions a large number of individual species. We shall therefore treat first the helminths in the human body, then those in the body of mammals, and finally those in the body of fish.
The Skin Worm.

Sometimes the worm מורנא is found between the foreskin and the glans of grown men, and it is removed by circumcision, through which the glans is laid bare. Many a heathen underwent circumcision as a consequence of this circumstance (A. Sara 26b). The name מורנא denotes yet another genus of helminths, on which see §. 482.
Phthiriasis.

The worm רמה sometimes comes out of the human body by the handful (Temura 31a); this is the well-known lousy disease, which has its seat either chiefly under the scalp or under the skin of the whole body.

From the tongues of the lying spies whom Moses sent to Canaan came forth חולעים, maggots (Sota 35a). This maggot is not to be confused with the phthiriasis mentioned in the preceding article, since the latter comes forth either from the skin, the folds of the skin, the ears, or the anus (Voigt l. c. 5. p. 409); it is rather the maggot that develops through a suppurating swelling.
A heretic had a discharge of maggots (מונק חולעים) from his nose (Jerusalem Talmud Joma 39a).
Corpse Maggot.

The maggot that develops from the human corpse is called רמה and תולע (Aboth 3, 1); the stouter the body, the more maggots it develops as a decayed corpse (ibid. 2, 7). In a corpse that had lain only a few days on a dunghill, maggots crept out of the nose (Joma 19b). In another corpse, which had remained unburied for a longer time, a worm (ריחשא) came out first from the ear (B. mez. 84b).
The Common Roundworm.

This worm, which is often present in the human intestines not singly but in great numbers, so that 56 roundworms were passed by a seven-year-old child (Voigt l. c. 6. p. 32), is called כירצא in the Talmud (Gittin 69b). As a remedy against it serves the consumption of ass's milk with laurel leaves (ארע = לורייר, Laurier, whose berry is called בייש, Baies, Gittin ibid.); further, the consumption of bread and salt taken on an empty stomach, and with it a drink of fresh water (B. mez. 107b).
The White Roundworm.

Since the common roundworm (§. 476) is reddish-brown, the white roundworm is called כירצא חיוורא (Gittin 69b). As a remedy against it serves the seed of spiny sea rocket (גילגולא = אורוגא, Spanish: Oruga, Latin: Eruca, French: Érucago; see Raschi on 2. Kön. 4, 39), which is wrapped in a cotton rag and softened in water, which is then drunk (Gittin ibid.). Might כירצא be related to Ascaris?
The Ascarid.

The small worms, very common especially in the rectum of children and passed in great numbers, are called כינים שבני מעיים (B. Kama 82a). The remedy against them is the consumption of garlic (ibid.), a household remedy that is still used today. The inhabitants of hot [p. 340] countries frequently eat garlic; see Jablonski: Allg. Lexicon s.v. Knoblauch.
The Tapeworm.

קוקיאני (Berachoth 36a), for which Aruch reads קקני. As a remedy against it is the consumption of raw barley meal (ibid.) and the consumption of hyssop (Sabbat 109b). The Mishna (Schebiith 7, 2) mentions a plant root רכפה, whose consumption kills the intestinal worms; see Bartenoro there.
The Human Liver Fluke.

Through frequent violations of diet, such as the consumption of roasted meat and water while one is still fasting, or through fat beef eaten before breakfast, worms arise in the human liver, which are called ארקא (Sabbat 109b). The remedy against them is the consumption of יעזר, which is explained by פוחנק. Raschi explains פוחנק by פולאל, Polegion, French: Pouliot, fleabane (ibid.).
Mussaphia does not think of worms here, but translates ארקתא by Aurigo, jaundice.
The Liver Fluke.

Chulin 48a speaks of החליע ככד, the “liver that has become wormy” of cattle; this is the liver fluke, Distoma hepaticum, which is sometimes found in great numbers in the liver of sheep and cattle (Voigt l. c. 6. p. 35).
The Sheep Worm.

Chulin 49a states that if the worm מורנא (§. 472) comes out of the lung of an animal, the animal is permitted to be eaten, because it is to be assumed that the worm left the lung only after the death of the animal, since during life the lung, strongly moved by breathing, does not permit the exit of the worm, [p. 341] and so the worm can have eaten through the lung and penetrated it only after death.
